rows.question: i have [[Hardened Scales]] and [[Doubling Season]] and cast ballista for X=2. how many counters does it come in with? do i get to pick the order or is it timestamps
rows.expected_answer: You choose the order and the best answer is 6. Walking Ballista's 'enters with X +1/+1 counters' is a replacement effect (614.1c, 614.12), and Hardened Scales and Doubling Season are further replacement effects modifying the same event. When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected permanent's controller picks which applies first (616.1), and since none of the special priorities in 616.1a-d apply, any may be chosen (616.1e). Each effect applies only once to the event (614.5). Apply Scales first (2 -> 3), then Season doubles (3 -> 6). Timestamps are irrelevant for replacement effects; that is the layer system for continuous effects.

outcome.answer:
You pick the order, not timestamps. Apply **Hardened Scales** first, then **Doubling Season**, and **Walking Ballista** enters with (2+1)×2 = **6** +1/+1 counters. If you apply Doubling Season first you get 2×2+1 = 5.

"This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it" is a replacement effect (614.1c), so the Ballista would enter with 2 counters. Both enchantments use "instead", which makes them replacement effects too (614.1a). The rulings confirm that both apply to counters a permanent enters with.

When two or more replacement effects try to modify the same event, the affected object's controller chooses which one to apply. Then the process repeats until there are none left to apply (616.1, 616.1f). Neither enchantment falls into the special categories that must go first, so you can choose either one (616.1e). Each effect applies only once (614.5). The Hardened Scales ruling says the same: "you choose the order to apply those effects."

The same goes for the {4} ability later. With Scales applied first, you get (1+1)×2 = 4 counters.
citations: rule 614.1c: "Effects that read “[This permanent] enters with . . . ,” “As [this permanent] enters . . . ,” or “[This permanent] enters as . . . “ are replacement effects."
rule 614.1a: "Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects."
rule 616.1: "the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply"
rule 616.1e: "Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen."
rule 616.1f: "Once the chosen effect has been applied, this process is repeated"
rule 614.5: "A replacement effect doesn’t invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event."
ruling a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6/636b245ed2960105: "you choose the order to apply those effects, no matter who controls the sources of those effects."
ruling 01546b7d-a233-4176-8843-d732074dc5b6/30e1af27509ea83b: "Doubling Season affects permanents that enter with counters."

rows.question: opp cast [[Blood Moon]] while i have all three tron lands out. do i still get my 7 mana from urza's? can i tap tower for 3 colorless or is it just a Mountain now
rows.expected_answer: Tron is off. Blood Moon is a type-changing effect (layer 4, 613.1d) that sets each nonbasic land's subtype to Mountain. Per 305.7, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type loses its old land types (so it is no longer an Urza's land), loses all abilities from its rules text (the colorless mana ability), and gains only '{T}: Add {R}'. Each Urza's land is a plain Mountain that taps for one red mana; Tower does not produce three because it no longer has that ability and the others no longer have the Urza's subtype. They are still nonbasic (305.8), so Blood Moon keeps affecting them.

outcome.answer:
No. Under **Blood Moon** each of your Tron lands is just a Mountain. It taps for {R} only, so all three together make {R}{R}{R}, not 7 colorless. **Urza's Tower** can't make {C}{C}{C}.

Why:
- Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." The Urza's lands aren't basic, so it applies to all three. This is a type-changing effect, which applies in layer 4 (`613.1d`).
- When an effect sets a subtype, the new one replaces the old land types (`205.1a`). So your lands lose Urza's Tower, Urza's Mine and Urza's Power-Plant as types.
- The Blood Moon ruling confirms that nonbasic lands "will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability "{T}: Add {R}.""

The Tron bonus is gone twice over. First, the lands no longer have their printed ability ("{T}: Add {C}. If you control an Urza's Mine and an Urza's Power-Plant, add {C}{C}{C} instead."). Second, even if they kept it, it looks for land types, not names, and no land has the Urza's types anymore.

They do keep their names (Blood Moon doesn't change names) and they're still nonbasic, but that doesn't bring the ability back.
citations: oracle 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae#0: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains."
rule 613.1d: "Layer 4: Type-changing effects are applied. These include effects that change an object’s card type, subtype, and/or supertype."
rule 205.1a: "when an effect sets one or more of an object’s subtypes, the new subtype(s) replaces any existing subtypes from the appropriate set"

ruling 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae/de7b24c7cfc8d0d2: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability \"{T}: Add {R}.\""
ruling 32fbb638-ab14-4e8b-a07a-d4c44e3496f2/67514ffa8ee40389: "The ability checks for land types, not the names of other permanents you control."

rows.question: follow up: what if I play [[Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth]] AFTER the moon is already down? urborg has the later timestamp so shouldn't it make everything a Swamp too? my friend says no
rows.expected_answer: Your friend is right. Both effects are layer 4 type-changing effects (613.1d). Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's (613.8a): applying Blood Moon makes Urborg a Mountain and strips its rules-text ability (305.7), which removes the existence of Urborg's effect. When a dependency exists it overrides timestamps (613.8), so Blood Moon applies first no matter which entered later (613.8b). Urborg is just a Mountain with '{T}: Add {R}' and nothing becomes a Swamp. (Any actual basic Swamps you control are still Swamps because Blood Moon only affects nonbasic lands.)

outcome.answer:
Your friend is right. With **Blood Moon** out, **Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth** makes nothing a Swamp, and it doesn't matter which one came down first.

Both effects are type-changing effects, so both apply in layer 4. Normally the later timestamp would win within a layer, but per `613.8` dependency "will override the timestamp system." Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's because applying Blood Moon "would change the text or the existence of the first effect" (`613.8a`). Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Urborg is a nonbasic land, so Blood Moon sets its land subtype to Mountain. Per `305.7`, that means Urborg "loses all abilities generated from its rules text." Blood Moon's effect doesn't depend on Urborg's, so it applies first. That strips Urborg's "Each land is a Swamp" ability before that ability can apply, which means Urborg's effect never exists.

The Scryfall ruling on Urborg says it outright: when an effect sets it to a basic land type, "it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply."

So Urborg is just a legendary Mountain that taps for {R}, and every other land stays as it would be without Urborg.
citations: rule 613.8: "If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system."
rule 613.8a: "applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to"
rule 305.7: "It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land"
oracle 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae#0: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains."
ruling db6174d7-211d-4817-b8e4-8384594c83f9/aebb4d57471c5c28: "it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply."

rows.question: my goyf has two +1/+1 counters on it and I just giant growthed it. opponent [[Clone]]s it. is their clone a huge goyf too or just a regular one? and does the clone even know how big a goyf should be since the p/t is */*+1
rows.expected_answer: Just a regular Tarmogoyf. A copy acquires only the copiable values of the original (707.2): name, mana cost, types, rules text, printed P/T, etc. Counters, Giant Growth's +3/+3, and other non-copy effects are not copiable values, so the Clone gets none of them. The Clone does copy Tarmogoyf's rules text, and therefore its characteristic-defining ability (707.2a), so the Clone's own P/T is */*+1 computed from card types in graveyards (applied in layer 7a, 613.4a). The copy effect itself is applied in layer 1a (613.2a); your goyf's counters and pump are layer 7c (613.4c) and stay on your goyf only.

outcome.answer:
Their **Clone** is just a regular Tarmogoyf. It doesn't get your counters or the Giant Growth bonus. It does copy Goyf's ability, though, so it will always be exactly as big as a fresh Goyf.

Per 707.2, a copy gets only the copiable values, meaning what's printed on the card (as modified by other copy effects). "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied." So the two +1/+1 counters stay on your Goyf. The +3/+3 from **Giant Growth** isn't copied either, because it's a non-copy effect. The Clone rulings say the same: it doesn't copy "whether it has any counters on it" or "any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness".

As for the */*+1: Goyf's power and toughness come from rules text, and a copy "acquires the abilities of the object it's copying because those values are derived from its rules text" (707.2a). So the Clone has "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1" and works it out on its own.

Example: if graveyards hold creature, instant and land, both Goyfs have a base size of 3/4. Yours is 8/9 this turn (+2/+2 from counters, +3/+3 from Giant Growth). Theirs is 3/4, and it grows or shrinks along with yours as the graveyards change. Once Giant Growth resolves, the instant is in the graveyard, and that counts for both of them.
citations: rule 707.2: "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied."
rule 707.2a: "A copy acquires the abilities of the object it’s copying because those values are derived from its rules text."

ruling 42226b87-0746-4ebf-9fd0-108d508462af/e115f2763b5d5e7e: "It doesn't copy whether that creature is tapped or untapped, whether it has any counters on it or Auras and Equipment attached to it, or any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness, types, color, or so on."
oracle 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd#0: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1."

rows.question: ok classic one. I have [[Humility]] out and my opponent drops [[Opalescence]]. what are Humility and Opalescence now?? are all my creatures still 1/1? does the answer change if Opalescence was out first?
rows.expected_answer: Walk the layers. Opalescence reads 'each OTHER non-Aura enchantment', so it never affects itself: Opalescence stays a noncreature enchantment and keeps its ability in every scenario. Layer 4 (613.1d): Opalescence makes Humility a 'creature' enchantment. Layer 6 (613.1f): Humility removes all abilities from every creature, including itself; per 613.6 an effect that has started applying keeps applying in later layers even though its source ability is gone. Layer 7b (613.4b): Humility's 'base P/T 1/1' and Opalescence's 'base P/T equal to mana value' both set Humility's P/T. Neither depends on the other under 613.8a (applying one doesn't change the text, existence, or targets of the other), so timestamp order decides (613.7). If Opalescence has the later timestamp: Humility is a 4/4 creature with no abilities. If Humility has the later timestamp: Humility is a 1/1 creature with no abilities. Either way every ordinary creature is a 1/1 with no abilities, and Opalescence is an unaffected noncreature enchantment. Any other non-Aura enchantment Opalescence animates follows Humility itself: its base power and toughness are its mana value when Opalescence is later, and 1/1 when Humility is.

outcome.answer:
Your regular creatures stay 1/1 with no abilities either way. Only the size of **Humility** depends on which enchantment came first. **Opalescence** stays a noncreature enchantment with its ability, because it says "Each other non-Aura enchantment", so it never animates itself and Humility can't touch it.

**Humility first, then Opalescence (your case):**
- Layer 4: Opalescence turns Humility into an enchantment creature.
- Layer 6: Humility removes all abilities from creatures, including its own. Per `613.6`, an effect that has started to apply keeps applying in the later layers "even if the ability generating the effect is removed during this process."
- Layer 7b: both effects set base P/T, so they apply in timestamp order (`613.4b`, `613.7`). Humility's 1/1 applies first, then Opalescence sets each other non-Aura enchantment to its mana value. Humility ends up a 4/4 with no abilities, and your other creatures are 1/1.

**Opalescence first, then Humility:** layers 4 and 6 work the same way. In 7b, Opalescence's effect applies first and Humility's later "1/1" overrides it, so Humility is a 1/1 with no abilities too.

The Scryfall ruling on the pair walks through exactly this: Humility becomes 4/4 if it entered first, and 1/1 if Opalescence entered first. Any other non-Aura enchantments on the battlefield work like Humility does: they're mana-value-sized if Humility is older, 1/1 if Humility is newer, and they lose their abilities in both cases.
citations: ruling ed7bdb3e-5c51-4547-9266-76a791e0b2b0/18649cad787b2eba: "The type-changing effect applies at layer 4, but the rest happens in the applicable layers. The rest of it will apply even if the permanent loses its ability before it's finished applying."

rule 613.6: "If an effect starts to apply in one layer and/or sublayer, it will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable layer and/or sublayer, even if the ability generating the effect is removed during this process."
rule 613.4b: "Layer 7b: Effects that set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value are applied. Effects that refer to the base power and/or toughness of a creature apply in this layer."
rule 613.7: "An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp."
oracle 59489b46-9d02-4f3c-bcd0-884e7605e9a5#0: "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value."

rows.question: quick one: if I have [[Valki, God of Lies]] in hand can I just cast the Tibalt side for 7? and while it's in my library/graveyard does it count as a planeswalker card for stuff like Vraska's Contempt / Kaya's Ghostform?
rows.expected_answer: Yes. Valki // Tibalt is a modal double-faced card: when you cast it you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack, and only that face is evaluated (712.11b, 712.11c), so you can cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for {5}{B}{R} straight from your hand. Once chosen, the spell/permanent has only that face's characteristics (712.8f). But anywhere other than the stack or battlefield (hand, library, graveyard, exile) an MDFC has only its front face's characteristics (712.8a), so it is a legendary creature card named Valki, God of Lies there — never a planeswalker card.

outcome.answer:
Yes. You can cast **Valki, God of Lies** as **Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor** straight from your hand for {5}{B}{R}. Per 712.11b you choose which face you're casting before the spell goes on the stack, and per 712.11c only that face is checked to see whether it can be cast.

In your library, graveyard or hand, though, it's only Valki. Per 712.8a, a double-faced card in any zone other than the battlefield or stack "has only the characteristics of its front face." So there it's a creature card with mana value 2, not a planeswalker card, and anything that looks for a "planeswalker card" in those zones won't find it. The Scryfall ruling confirms this: "In all other zones, consider only the front face."

Neither of your examples actually looks at cards in those zones. **Vraska's Contempt** ("Exile target creature or planeswalker") and **Kaya's Ghostform** ("Enchant creature or planeswalker you control") both deal with permanents on the battlefield. Per 712.8f, a modal double-faced permanent has only the characteristics of the face that's up. So if you cast it as Tibalt, it's a planeswalker for both cards. If you cast it as Valki, it's a creature, which those cards can also affect.
citations: rule 712.11b: "A player casting a modal double-faced card or a copy of a modal double-faced card as a spell chooses which face they are casting before putting it onto the stack."
rule 712.8a: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face."
rule 712.8f: "While a modal double-faced spell is on the stack or a modal double-faced permanent is on the battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that’s up."
ruling 907ae517-22d5-4ac7-bc3a-3f4d5eaeeb57/37339bfb61f528f0: "In all other zones, consider only the front face."
rule 712.11c: "Only the face that will be face up on the stack is evaluated to determine if it can be cast."

rows.question: cast Stomp off my bonecrusher giant, it resolved and went to exile. my opp says I can only cast the creature half from exile now, not Stomp again, is that right? also can they counter Stomp with a 'counter target creature spell' effect since the card is a creature?
rows.expected_answer: Your opponent is right. When an Adventure spell resolves it is exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and you may cast the card from exile — but only as the creature (Bonecrusher Giant), not as Stomp again (715.3d). And no, Stomp can't be hit by 'counter target creature spell': while on the stack as an Adventure the spell has only its alternative characteristics (715.3a, 715.3b), so it is a red instant, not a creature spell. Everywhere else, including exile, the card is just the creature card Bonecrusher Giant (715.4).

outcome.answer:
Your opponent is right on the first point, and the answer to the second is no.

**Exile:** After **Stomp** resolves, the card goes to exile, and while it stays there you may play it, but only as **Bonecrusher Giant**. Per 715.3d: "It can’t be cast as an Adventure this way, although other effects that allow a player to cast it may allow a player to cast it as an Adventure." So you can't cast Stomp again from that exile unless some other effect lets you. You still follow normal timing when you cast the Giant, which usually means your main phase with an empty stack.

**'Counter target creature spell':** That can't target Stomp. While a spell cast as an Adventure is on the stack, it has only its alternative characteristics (715.3b). The Scryfall ruling says to "use the alternative characteristics and ignore all of the card's normal characteristics." On the stack, Stomp is an instant, not a creature spell. The card counts as a creature card in every other zone (715.4), which is why a creature-spell counter works on the Giant when you cast it from exile later.

If Stomp gets countered some other way, it goes to your graveyard instead of exile, and you lose the chance to cast the Giant from exile.
citations: rule 715.3d: "It can’t be cast as an Adventure this way, although other effects that allow a player to cast it may allow a player to cast it as an Adventure."
rule 715.3b: "While on the stack as an Adventure, the spell has only its alternative characteristics."
rule 715.4: "In every zone except the stack, and while on the stack not as an Adventure, an adventurer card has only its normal characteristics."
ruling d6d72f5f-8f5d-4180-b514-f22ff5482902/700df45a4e7078ff: "When casting a spell as an Adventure, use the alternative characteristics and ignore all of the card's normal characteristics."

ruling d6d72f5f-8f5d-4180-b514-f22ff5482902/9f9546560bbab6ce: "If an Adventure spell leaves the stack in any way other than resolving (most likely by being countered or by failing to resolve because its targets have all become illegal), that card won't be exiled"

rows.question: melded my Bruna and Gisela into Brisela and then it got Path to Exiled. does that count as one creature leaving or two for my [[Blood Artist]] type triggers, and do I get one Plains or two off Path?
rows.expected_answer:
Blood Artist does not trigger at all here: Path to Exile exiles Brisela, and Blood Artist
triggers on a creature dying, which means being put into a graveyard from the battlefield
(700.4). Exile is not dying. If Brisela instead died (say, to a Wrath of God), Blood Artist
would trigger exactly once: one permanent left the battlefield, even though the melded
permanent is a single object represented by two cards (712.21, 701.42a). A trigger reading
"whenever a card is put into a graveyard" would see two cards (712.21e). Either way, the
search happens once and Bruna and Gisela both go to exile. It is Brisela's controller who
searches, not the player who cast Path to Exile ("Its controller may search their library
for a basic land card"), and any basic land will do, not only a Plains.

outcome.answer:
It counts as one creature leaving, and Path gets you one basic land. Also, **Blood Artist** itself won't trigger at all here. It triggers when a creature "dies", and being exiled is not dying.

Per `712.21`, when a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, "one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone." The CR's own example says a "whenever a creature dies" trigger triggers once for a melded permanent. A "whenever a card is put into a graveyard from anywhere" trigger would trigger twice. So if Brisela had died instead, Blood Artist would trigger once. Any "whenever a creature leaves the battlefield" or "is exiled" trigger also sees just one creature. Per `712.21e`, anything that counts objects counts the melded permanent as one object, and anything that counts cards counts two.

**Path to Exile** targets and exiles one creature, then says "Its controller may search their library for a basic land card". That's a single search for a single basic land card, no matter how many physical cards made up the creature. `712.21c` only means that effects acting on the exiled cards act on both of them. Path's search isn't done to the exiled cards, so there is still only one search. You get one Plains (or any other basic).
citations: rule 712.21: "If a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone."

rule 712.21: "Example: Chittering Host, a melded permanent, dies. An ability that triggers “whenever a creature dies” triggers once. An ability that triggers “whenever a card is put into a graveyard from anywhere” triggers twice."
rule 712.21e: "If an effect needs to know the number of objects that changed zones, a melded permanent among those objects counts as one object that moved."
rule 712.21c: "If an effect can find the new object that a melded permanent becomes as it leaves the battlefield, it finds both cards."
oracle d683d985-9888-4d21-8b5f-69e69ce4a03b#0: "Exile target creature. Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle."
oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."

rows.question: old school question. my Waylay (Urza's Saga printing) says 'at end of turn, remove them from the game'. so I cast it during my opponent's end step, the knights survive since the end step already started, and I get to swing with them on my turn right? classic waylay trick
rows.expected_answer: No — that trick was closed by errata. The printed text is not what the card does; you always use the current Oracle wording (108.1), which is 'Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step.' If you cast Waylay in your opponent's end step, the Knights are exiled at that same turn's cleanup step: the game checks for triggered abilities waiting during cleanup, puts the 'beginning of the next cleanup step' trigger on the stack, and then players get priority and another cleanup step follows (514.3a). You never get to attack with them. (Casting it during your opponent's declare-attackers step to get surprise blockers still works.)

outcome.answer:
No, that trick doesn't work anymore. **Waylay** has Oracle errata. Its current text reads "Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step." Cards printed with "at end of turn" were errata'd (`513.1a`), and Waylay's exile now happens in the cleanup step, which shuts down this exact play.

The cleanup step comes straight after the end step in the same turn: "The ending phase consists of two steps: end and cleanup" (`512.1`). So if you cast Waylay during your opponent's end step, the next cleanup step is that same turn's cleanup. When it starts, the game checks whether "any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”)". If so, the trigger goes on the stack, players get priority, the Knights are exiled, and then another cleanup step begins (`514.3a`).

The Knights only last for the rest of your opponent's turn. You can use them as surprise blockers if you cast Waylay earlier, or as sacrifice fodder, but they never make it to your turn.
citations: oracle f0db78c7-09b5-4981-8ca8-6dbab597c5d9#0: "Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step."
rule 513.1a: "Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference"
rule 512.1: "The ending phase consists of two steps: end and cleanup."

rule 514.3a: "At this point, the game checks to see if any state-based actions would be performed and/or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”)."

rows.question: my mirage LED says 'play this ability as an interrupt'. so it's a mana ability and I can crack it in the middle of casting Infernal Tutor to pay for it right? that way I still have tutor as the last card when I discard
rows.expected_answer: No. Ignore the printed 'interrupt' text and use the current Oracle wording (108.1): 'Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant.' It is still a mana ability — the timing restriction doesn't change that (605.1) — but 'Activate only as an instant' means you may only activate it when you have priority (602.5e), so you can't activate it while paying for a spell the way 605.3a normally allows for mana abilities. The correct play is to cast Infernal Tutor with Tutor as the last card in hand, hold priority, then activate LED in response; when Tutor resolves you are hellbent and the mana is still floating.

outcome.answer:
No. **Lion's Eye Diamond** is a mana ability, but you can't activate it while you're in the middle of casting **Infernal Tutor**. The current Oracle text replaces the old "interrupt" wording: "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant."

The restriction doesn't stop it from being a mana ability. Per `605.1`, abilities that meet the criteria are mana abilities "regardless of … what timing restrictions (such as "Activate only as an instant") they may have." The Scryfall ruling agrees: it resolves as a mana ability "but it can only be activated at times when you can cast an instant."

Normally `605.3a` lets you activate a mana ability partway through casting a spell. LED's restriction overrides that. Per `602.5e`, "Activate only as an instant" means you must follow instant timing, which means you need priority. You don't have priority in the middle of casting a spell.

You also don't need that trick. The first step of casting Tutor moves it from your hand to the stack (`601.2a`), so it isn't in your hand when LED's cost discards your hand.

The correct line: cast Tutor using other mana, hold priority, then crack LED in response. Tutor then resolves with Hellbent live ("If you have no cards in hand, instead search your library for a card"). LED's three mana will be in your pool for whatever you do next in that step.
citations: oracle ee6099b0-fb1f-42f1-b862-7708c6e36d05#0: "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant."
rule 602.5e: "Activated abilities that read “Activate only as an instant” mean the player must follow the timing rules for casting an instant spell, though the ability isn’t actually an instant."

ruling ee6099b0-fb1f-42f1-b862-7708c6e36d05/311e9a5aa9d6c7d6: "The ability is a mana ability, so it is activated and resolves as a mana ability, but it can only be activated at times when you can cast an instant."

rows.question: ok so I have [[Blood Artist]] out and my opponent wraths with [[Wrath of God]]. Blood Artist dies at the same time as everything else so does it even see the other creatures die? do I drain for all of them or just itself?
rows.expected_answer: Yes, you drain for every creature that died, including Blood Artist itself. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities 'look back in time' (603.10, 603.6c): the game checks the state immediately before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield, so it sees every creature that died simultaneously, including itself. All those triggers go on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (603.3), and you choose a target player for each one.

outcome.answer:
You drain for all of them. **Blood Artist** triggers once for each creature that dies to **Wrath of God**, and that includes Blood Artist itself.

A "dies" trigger is a leaves-the-battlefield ability. For those, the game "looks back in time" per `603.10a`, checking what was on the battlefield just before the event. Blood Artist was there when the creatures were destroyed, so it sees every one of them die, even though it goes to the graveyard at the same moment. The CR example under 603.10a covers exactly this: an artifact with "Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life" still triggers for each creature when it's destroyed along with them.

One event with several deaths gives several triggers, per `603.2c`: "it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences." The Scryfall ruling confirms it: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."

So if 5 creatures died in total, counting Blood Artist, you get 5 triggers. Each one reads "target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life," and you choose the target separately for each trigger as it goes on the stack.
citations: rule 603.10a: "Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities"
rule 603.2c: "However, it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences."
ruling 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d/eaf0e0e76c3621ab: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."
oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."

rows.question: my buddy says once I cast a spell he can't respond until I 'pass'. I cast Lightning Bolt at his bob, do I get to keep going and cast a second Bolt before he gets a chance to counter the first one?
rows.expected_answer: Your buddy is half right. After you cast a spell you receive priority again (117.3c), so you may cast the second Bolt immediately, before he can respond to the first. He only gets priority when you pass. Nothing resolves until all players pass in succession with the stack non-empty (117.4); then only the top object resolves, and the active player gets priority again after it resolves (117.3b). So he can still respond to either Bolt once you pass, but you are entitled to stack both first.

outcome.answer:
Yes. After you cast the first **Lightning Bolt**, you get priority again, so you can cast a second Bolt on top of it before your buddy gets a chance to do anything. Per `601.2i`, "If the spell's controller had priority before casting it, they get priority." `117.3c` says the same thing. Your opponent only gets priority when you pass (`117.3d`). A spell resolves only when all players pass in succession (`117.4`).

So if you cast Bolt #1 and then Bolt #2 while holding priority, both are on the stack when you finally pass. Your buddy can then respond, for example by countering either one. The stack resolves last-in, first-out (`405.5`), so if he does nothing, Bolt #2 resolves first. After that he gets another chance to respond before Bolt #1 resolves, because the active player gets priority again after each resolution (`117.3b`) and everyone has to pass again.

Your buddy is right that he can't respond until you pass. He's wrong if he thinks that means he gets a window between your two Bolts: he doesn't. If Bob dies to the second Bolt, the first one's only target is gone when it tries to resolve, so it doesn't resolve (`608.2b`).
citations: rule 601.2i: "If the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority."
rule 117.3c: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward."
rule 117.3d: "If a player has priority and chooses not to take any actions, that player passes."
rule 117.4: "If all players pass in succession (that is, if all players pass without taking any actions in between passing), the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves"
rule 405.5: "When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves."
rule 117.3b: "The active player receives priority after a spell or ability (other than a mana ability) resolves."
rule 608.2b: "If all its targets, for every instance of the word “target,” are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn’t resolve."

rows.question: I control a 2/2 with a Giant Growth resolving on it, and mid-resolution of a different spell it's technically at 0 toughness for a second (Maro-style hand-size thing). Does it die? And separately, if I have two Ragavan on the battlefield somehow, when exactly does the legend rule kick in - can I respond in between?
rows.expected_answer: 1) It doesn't die. State-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, not in the middle of a spell resolving (704.3, 704.4 - the CR's own Maro example). The creature only dies if it still has toughness 0 or less when SBAs are next checked (704.5f). 2) The legend rule (704.5j) is also a state-based action: the moment a player would get priority with two Ragavans you control, you choose one and the other goes to the graveyard. It doesn't use the stack and there is no window to respond between the second Ragavan entering and the legend rule applying; you can only respond before the second one enters/resolves.

outcome.answer:
No, it doesn't die, as long as its toughness is back above 0 by the time the spell finishes resolving. And with two **Ragavan**, the legend rule is applied before anyone gets priority, so there's no window to respond.

**Toughness 0 mid-resolution:** State-based actions are only checked when a player would get priority (`704.3`), and "state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability" (`704.4`). The 0-toughness rule in `704.5f` only looks at the creature when that check happens. The **Maro** example in `704.4` is exactly this case: Maro drops to 0 toughness partway through the spell, is back up to 7 when it finishes, and survives. Maro's ruling says the same. The creature would die only if its toughness were still 0 or less when the spell finished resolving.

**Two Ragavans:** The legend rule is a state-based action (`704.5j`). If you control two legendary permanents with the same name, you choose one and the rest go to the graveyard. State-based actions don't use the stack (`704.1`). They're performed before a player would receive priority (`117.2d`), and the game repeats the check until nothing more happens before anyone gets priority (`704.3`). So the moment the second Ragavan is on the battlefield, the next check happens before anyone can act. You can't respond to the legend rule itself. You can only respond before the second Ragavan arrives, for example while its spell is still on the stack. Any leaves-the-battlefield or dies triggers from the Ragavan you put in the graveyard go on the stack afterward.
citations: rule 704.4: "Unlike triggered abilities, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability."
rule 704.5f: "If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard."
ruling ef32258a-d567-4fbc-ab85-8c00080f5b36/654c63e82671903c: "Creatures are only put into a graveyard for having 0 toughness when state-based actions are checked."
rule 704.5j: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards."
rule 704.1: "State-based actions don’t use the stack."
rule 117.2d: "State-based actions happen automatically when certain conditions are met. See rule 704. They’re dealt with before a player would receive priority."

rule 704.3: "Whenever a player would get priority (see rule 117, “Timing and Priority”), the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event."

rows.question: I attack with a 5/5 trample that also has deathtouch (Questing Beast) and they block with a 4/4. how much can I trample over? my opponent says I have to assign 4 to the blocker first
rows.expected_answer: The premise is off: Questing Beast is a 4/4 with vigilance, deathtouch and haste, and it does not have trample, so blocked by one creature it assigns all its combat damage to that blocker and nothing goes to the player (510.1c). A good answer says so. For the creature the asker describes, a 5/5 with trample and deathtouch, you only need to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 and can trample 4 over to the player. Trample requires lethal damage to be assigned to all blockers before excess goes to the player (702.19b), but any nonzero damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for that purpose (702.2c). Damage assignment for a blocked creature follows 510.1c, then all combat damage is dealt simultaneously with no chance to respond in between (510.2). The 4/4 is then destroyed by deathtouch as an SBA.

outcome.answer:
With deathtouch and trample you only need to assign **1** damage to the 4/4. The other 4 can trample over to the player (or planeswalker) you're attacking. Your opponent is wrong.

Per `702.19b`, a trampler has to assign lethal damage to its blockers before any excess can go to the player, and `702.2c` says "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt." So 1 damage counts as lethal to the 4/4, and the rest is excess you can assign however you like between the blocker and the player. The 1 point still destroys the 4/4 thanks to deathtouch (`702.2b`).

One correction: **Questing Beast**'s current Oracle text doesn't include trample. Its keywords are only "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste". Without trample from some other source, a blocked Beast deals all its damage to the blocker and none to the player (`510.1c`). If it does have trample, its other line "Combat damage that would be dealt by creatures you control can't be prevented" also applies. Any combat damage the Beast deals to the opponent triggers its last ability, which deals the same amount to a target planeswalker that player controls.
citations: rule 702.2c: "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt."

rule 702.19b: "Once all those blocking creatures are assigned lethal damage, any excess damage is assigned as its controller chooses among those blocking creatures and the player, planeswalker, or battle the creature is attacking."
rule 702.2b: "A creature with toughness greater than 0 that’s been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch since the last time state-based actions were checked is destroyed as a state-based action."
oracle b685757b-521e-4353-a233-97052359723d#0: "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste"
rule 510.1c: "If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature."

rows.question: commander q: my commander is [[Kenrith, the Returned King]]. two things: 1) can I run Nicol Bolas, the Ravager since Kenrith's text mentions all 5 colors? and 2) someone bounced Kenrith to my hand with Unsummon - does he go to the command zone or is that only for graveyard/exile?
rows.expected_answer: 1) Yes. Color identity includes mana symbols in the mana cost AND in the rules text (903.4), so Kenrith's identity is WUBRG even though his mana cost is only {4}{W}. Nicol Bolas, the Ravager (UBR) is legal because every color in its identity is in Kenrith's (903.5c). 2) Yes, Kenrith can go to the command zone. If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead - a replacement effect (903.9b). Graveyard/exile use a separate state-based action (903.9a). Either way it's optional.

outcome.answer:
1) Yes. **Kenrith, the Returned King** has all five colors in his color identity, so **Nicol Bolas, the Ravager** is legal in your deck. 2) If Kenrith is returned to your hand, you may put him into the command zone instead. That option isn't limited to the graveyard and exile.

**Color identity:** Per `903.4`, a card's color identity includes "the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text". Kenrith costs {4}{W}, and his abilities use {R}, {G}, {W}, {U} and {B}, so his identity is WUBRG. Bolas's identity is blue, black and red. That comes from the {1}{U}{B}{R} front and the back face, which counts per `903.4d`. `903.5c` only requires that every color in a card's identity also appears in your commander's identity, and it does.

**Unsummon:** Hand and library are covered by a separate rule from graveyard and exile. `903.9b` says: "If a commander would be put into its owner’s hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead." This is a replacement, so you decide as **Unsummon** resolves. You can let Kenrith go to your hand and recast him from there without commander tax, or send him to the command zone. The graveyard/exile version in `903.9a` is instead a state-based action that you choose after he gets there. Tax only counts casts from the command zone (`903.8`).
citations: rule 903.4: "The color identity of a card is the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text"
rule 903.4d: "The back face of a double-faced card (see rule 712) is included when determining a card’s color identity."
rule 903.5c: "A card can be included in a Commander deck only if every color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck’s commander."
rule 903.9b: "If a commander would be put into its owner’s hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead."
rule 903.9a: "If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone."
rule 903.8: "A commander cast from the command zone costs an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game."

rows.question: commander damage question. I've been hit for 15 by my opponent's Rafiq. she then copies it with a Clone and hits me for 6 more with the clone. do I lose? also does the 21 count noncombat damage like from Fling?
rows.expected_answer: No to both. A player loses when they've been dealt 21 or more COMBAT damage by the SAME commander over the course of the game (903.10a; checked as a state-based action, 704.6c). The Clone copying Rafiq is not a commander, so its 6 damage isn't commander damage - you're still at 15 from the real Rafiq. Fling damage is noncombat, so it never counts toward the 21 either; it just reduces your life total normally.

outcome.answer:
No, you don't lose. The Clone is not her commander, so its 6 damage doesn't count toward the 21. Fling damage doesn't count either, because only combat damage counts.

The commander designation belongs to the card itself and is not a characteristic that can be copied (903.3). The rule even gives the example that "A permanent that’s copying a commander ... is not a commander." A **Clone** copying **Rafiq of the Many** is just a Rafiq-shaped creature. Its damage is ordinary damage: it lowers your life total, but it doesn't add to the commander-damage count. That count also tracks each commander separately. Per 903.10a, you lose if you've been "dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game." So you're still at 15 from the real Rafiq.

On **Fling**: 903.10a counts only combat damage. If she Flings Rafiq (or anything else) at you, it's normal damage that makes you lose that much life (119.2). It adds nothing to the commander-damage total, even if the creature she sacrificed was her commander. Of course, all that damage still comes off your 40 life, and you lose at 0 or less life (119.6).

Watch out if the real Rafiq attacks alone. Its trigger says it "gains double strike until end of turn," and exalted gives it +1/+1. That's easily enough to cover the 6 you have left.
citations: rule 903.3: "A permanent that’s copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player’s graveyard) is not a commander."
rule 903.10a: "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game."
rule 119.2: "Damage dealt to a player normally causes that player to lose that much life."
rule 119.6: "If a player has 0 or less life, that player loses the game as a state-based action."
oracle c6e17443-2379-419d-8c32-13ea9bf52993#0: "Whenever a creature you control attacks alone, it gains double strike until end of turn."

rows.question: two quick ones. 1) if I tap all my lands during my upkeep does that mana stick around so I can cast the mind sculptor in my main phase? 2) when I'm casting snappy can I tap lands in the middle of casting it or do I have to float the mana first?
rows.expected_answer: 1) No. Each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, so mana added during your upkeep is lost before your main phase (106.4). Tap the lands in your main phase instead. 2) Yes. Casting a spell includes a step where, if the total cost includes mana, you get a chance to activate mana abilities such as tapping lands (601.2g), and only then do you pay the total cost (601.2h). You do not need to float mana before announcing the spell.

outcome.answer:
1) No. Mana tapped in your upkeep is gone by the time you reach your main phase, so you can't use it for **Jace, the Mind Sculptor**. Per `106.4`, "Each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase." The mana drains when upkeep ends, so it won't even last into your draw step. Tap for Jace in the main phase you cast him.

2) You don't need to float mana first. Tapping lands partway through casting **Snapcaster Mage** is the normal way to do it. Per `601.2g`, once the total cost is set, "the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities," and those have to be activated before the costs are paid. Per `605.3a`, you can activate mana abilities "whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment." So you announce Snapcaster, the cost is locked in, and then you tap your lands and pay. Floating mana first also works, but only within the same step or phase.
citations: rule 106.4: "Each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana."

rule 601.2g: "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid."
rule 605.3a: "A player may activate an activated mana ability whenever they have priority, whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment"

rows.question: my opp has [[bob]] and flipped a tim off the top, then next turn he flipped a goyf. how much life does he lose each time? goyf is like a 5/6 rn so is it 5?
rows.expected_answer: Dark Confidant makes you lose life equal to the revealed card's mana value, which is the total mana in its mana cost regardless of color (202.3). Prodigal Sorcerer costs {2}{U}, so he loses 3 life. Tarmogoyf costs {1}{G}, so he loses 2 life. Tarmogoyf's power/toughness is irrelevant; mana value is based only on the mana cost.

outcome.answer:
He loses 3 life for the **Prodigal Sorcerer** ("Tim") and 2 for the **Tarmogoyf**. Goyf's current size doesn't matter.

**Dark Confidant** has you "reveal the top card of your library and put that card into your hand. You lose life equal to its mana value." Per `202.3`, mana value is "the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color." Tim costs {2}{U}, so its mana value is 3. Goyf costs {1}{G}, so its mana value is 2.

Goyf's 5/6 comes from its characteristic-defining ability (`208.2a`), which only sets its power and toughness: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1." It has no effect on its mana cost, so Bob's trigger doesn't look at its power at all.
citations: rule 202.3: "The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color."
oracle 2068185c-1b50-47d0-aa3f-bf505d199428#0: "reveal the top card of your library and put that card into your hand. You lose life equal to its mana value."
rule 208.2a: "The card may have a characteristic-defining ability that sets its power and/or toughness according to some stated condition."
oracle 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd#0: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1."
